question: Friction
content: Friction is the resistive force created when two surfaces slide past each other, converting useful kinetic energy into wasted thermal energy. In human systems, it manifests as bureaucracy, legal hurdles, and interpersonal friction that sap productive energy.
description: A product team notices that 60% of customers who add items to their cart never complete checkout. The checkout flow has seven screens, five form fields per screen, and no guest checkout option. What is the core problem?
options: Customers are not genuinely interested in the products
The prices are too high compared to competitors
Checkout friction converts potential revenue into lost energy
The website loads too slowly for most users
answer: Checkout friction converts potential revenue into lost energy
explanation: Like physical friction that turns kinetic energy into heat, each extra screen and form field in the checkout flow converts customer purchase intent into frustration and abandonment. The fix is not more marketing — it is removing friction points.

question: Viscosity
content: Viscosity is internal friction within a system — a measure of how easily a fluid flows. In organizations, high viscosity means sluggish decision-making where even simple initiatives grind to a halt regardless of how much pressure is applied.
description: Two mid-sized companies try to adopt AI tools. Company A rolls out a company-wide AI policy in six weeks. Company B is still in the 'approval committee formation' phase after six months. What distinguishes them?
options: Company A had a larger budget for AI tools which influences how the overall
Company A flows easily with low viscosity, Company B stays stuck
Company A's employees are more technically skilled
Company B's industry is more regulated
answer: Company A flows easily with low viscosity, Company B stays stuck
explanation: Viscosity describes how easily an organization flows. High-viscosity cultures grind initiatives to a halt through endless committees, sign-offs, and red tape. Low-viscosity organizations move quickly because internal resistance is minimal.

question: Friction Audit
content: To optimize any system, do not simply add more force — instead, systematically identify and remove hidden friction points. The smoothest systems win by minimizing resistance, not maximizing raw power.
description: Your support team is overwhelmed with tickets about password resets. Engineering proposes building a sophisticated AI bot to handle the volume. What approach does the friction model suggest first?
options: Build the AI bot — automation is always the right solution
Hire more support agents to handle the ticket volume
Conduct a friction audit: find root cause of password resets
Outsource password reset support to a third-party vendor
answer: Conduct a friction audit: find root cause of password resets
explanation: Adding AI force treats the symptom, not the cause. A friction audit would examine why password resets are frequent — perhaps the expiration policy is too aggressive, or the reset flow itself is confusing. Removing the underlying friction eliminates the problem entirely.

question: Surface Area and Friction
content: The larger the contact surface between two objects, the greater the friction. In organizations, the more touchpoints and handoffs between teams, the more energy is lost in coordination overhead.
description: A company splits into eight micro-teams each owning a small piece of the product. Feature delivery slows dramatically despite all teams being fully staffed. What explains this?
options: Micro-teams are inherently less productive than larger teams which affects how the individuals
Coordination friction from more team interfaces wastes energy on handoffs
Developers in micro-teams lose their specialization
The product architecture does not support micro-team ownership
answer: Coordination friction from more team interfaces wastes energy on handoffs
explanation: Each handoff between teams is a contact surface that generates friction. More teams mean more surfaces, more meetings, more context-switching, and more energy lost to coordination. Sometimes reducing the number of interfaces improves total system throughput.

question: Lubrication
content: Introducing a lubricant between two surfaces dramatically reduces friction. In human systems, lubrication takes the form of standardized processes, clear APIs, shared tooling, and aligned incentives.
description: A design team and an engineering team constantly clash over handoff quality. Designs are ambiguous, engineers build the wrong thing, and rework piles up. What is the most effective lubricant for this interface?
options: Replace the design team with engineers who can design their own interfaces
Require all designs to be pixel-perfect before any engineering work begins
Create shared design system, handoff protocols, and cross-functional review reducing translation loss
Have the engineering manager sit in every design review and approve each decision
answer: Create shared design system, handoff protocols, and cross-functional review reducing translation loss
explanation: Just as oil reduces metal-on-metal friction, shared tooling and protocols reduce the friction between teams. A design system eliminates ambiguity; clear handoff protocols reduce rework. The goal is to minimize the energy lost in translation between functions.

question: Friction vs Force Trade-off
content: When a system has high friction, leaders often respond by applying more force — more pressure, more hours, more spending. This approach is wasteful; reducing friction is almost always more efficient than increasing force.
description: The VP of Sales keeps pushing the team to make more calls, extending targets, and hiring more representatives — yet revenue per rep keeps declining. What is the VP missing?
options: The sales team is not motivated enough and needs better incentives given the dynamics of the
The sales reps are not sufficiently trained on product features
Sales process friction — lead quality, CRM, and compensation — force cannot fix
The market has shifted and the product is no longer viable
answer: Sales process friction — lead quality, CRM, and compensation — force cannot fix
explanation: Adding more force (more reps, more calls) to a high-friction system yields diminishing returns. A friction audit would reveal the actual bottlenecks — perhaps reps waste hours on CRM data entry or receive low-quality leads. Removing those friction points increases output without more force.

question: Cultural Viscosity and Innovation
content: High-viscosity cultures resist novel ideas regardless of merit. An innovation may have overwhelming evidence supporting it, but it will not flow through a thick organizational culture.
description: A mid-level manager discovers a competitor's successful pricing model and presents data showing it would increase revenue by 15%. The idea dies in committee review for six months. What is the root cause?
options: The data was not convincing enough to justify the change
The competitor's pricing model would not work for this specific industry
High cultural viscosity traps even well-supported ideas in approval
The manager did not present the idea to the right stakeholders
answer: High cultural viscosity traps even well-supported ideas in approval
explanation: In a high-viscosity culture, ideas do not flow based on merit alone. They get trapped by hierarchy, risk aversion, and process overhead. Reducing viscosity means flattening approval chains, empowering decision-making at lower levels, and creating rapid experimentation pathways.

question: Smooth Systems Win
content: The most effective systems are not the most powerful — they are the ones with the least internal resistance. A frictionless system outperforms a powerful but sticky system every time.
description: Two ride-sharing apps operate in the same city. App A has more drivers and lower prices. App B has fewer drivers but a simpler interface, faster matching, and fewer cancellation steps. App B has higher customer satisfaction. What does this illustrate?
options: Customers prefer smaller companies over market leaders
A smoother, lower-friction experience can compensate for less raw power in the network
App A's drivers are less professional than App B's drivers which influences how the overall system
App A's prices are too low and attract low-quality riders
answer: A smoother, lower-friction experience can compensate for less raw power in the network
explanation: App A applies more force (more drivers, lower prices) but App B reduces friction (simpler flow, faster matching). The smoother system wins because it wastes less user energy. This is the essence of the friction model — minimizing resistance often beats maximizing force.
